We have a task: identify the compound from experimental data. We have mass spec: m/z 193.1103 (intensity 100) etc. Likely molecular ion at 193.1103. The formula we derived from isomers list: C11H15NO2 (exact mass? Let's compute: C11=132.0, H15=15.117, N=14.003, O2=31.998 => total 193.118 approx. The observed 193.1103 close. So formula C11H15NO2.

We have carbon NMR experimental: Deltas: 166.40, 144.78, 132.00, 130.07, 130.07, 127.80, 127.80, 52.24, 49.55, 43.55, 19.23.

We need to match to a structure.

We have candidate isomers from list. Need to find which matches carbon NMR.

Carbon NMR shows a carbonyl around 166 ppm (likely amide carbonyl). Aromatic carbons: many around 130-145. Two identical pairs at 130.07 (two) and 127.80 (two) suggests symmetric aromatic ring? Possibly para-substituted phenyl with two sets of equivalent carbons.

Also a carbon at 144.78 maybe aromatic carbon attached to hetero (e.g., N). 166.40 carbonyl.

Aliphatic carbons: 52.24, 49.55, 43.55, 19.23. These could be O-CH2 (52), N-CH2 (49), maybe a tertiary carbon (43) and methyl (19). So maybe an ethoxy group (CH3-CH2-O) gives CH3 ~19, CH2 ~52. N-CH2 maybe ~49. Tertiary carbon (C attached to carbonyl and two alkyl groups) ~43.

Thus structure could be ethyl ester? But carbonyl is amide (C=O attached to N). Ethoxy attached to carbonyl? Actually O-CH2-CH3 would give carbonyl of ester ~170, but we have 166 typical for amide.

So maybe N-ethyl, O-ethyl? Wait O-CH2 at 52 suggests O-CH2 attached to carbonyl (i.e., O-CH2-CH3 of ethyl ester). But carbonyl at 166 is lower than typical ester (170-175). Amide carbonyl ~165-170. So could be N-acetyl? But O-CH2 at 52 suggests O-CH2 attached to carbonyl (ester). So maybe it's an ethyl carbamate (urethane) - O-CH2CH3 attached to carbonyl, N attached to something else.

C11H15NO2: Could be ethyl phenylcarbamate? Phenyl carbamate: O=C(OC2H5)N-Ph. That would be C9H9NO2? Actually phenyl (C6H5) + OCOEt (C3H5O2) + N? Let's compute: phenyl (C6H5) + carbonyl carbon (C) + O (O) + OCH2CH3 (C2H5O) + N (N) = C9? Wait: O=C(OC2H5)N-Ph: total C = 6 (phenyl) + 1 (carbonyl) + 2 (ethyl) = 9. That's C9H? Not 11. So need extra carbon.

Maybe N,N-dimethyl? But formula includes only one N, two O, 11 C. Could be ethyl 2-phenylacetamide? That is C10H13NO? Not.

Let's compute formula for ethyl 2-phenylpropionate? That's C11H14O2, no N.

Our formula includes N, so maybe anilide with ethoxy substituent on carbonyl: ethyl 4-aminobenzamide? Wait.

Consider structure: ethyl 4-aminobenzamide (C9?). Actually 4-aminobenzamide is C7H8NO2? Not.

Let's examine candidate isomers list. Which have carbonyl amide and ethoxy? First candidate: "CCOC1=C(C=CC=N1)C(=O)C(C)C". That's a pyridine ring with ethoxy attached to aromatic, carbonyl attached to isopropyl. Contains N in ring, not amide. Carbonyl attached to isopropyl (ketone). Not match carbonyl at 166 (ketone ~200). So not.

Second: "CC1(CC2=C(CCC(=O)N2)C(=O)C1)C". Complex.

Third: "CC1=C(C=CC=C1O)C2COCCN2". Contains phenol and morpholine.

Fourth: "CN(C)[C@H]1[C@H](COC2=CC=CC=C12)O". Contains dimethylamino.

Fifth: "CN(C)CCC1=C2C(=CC=C1)OCO2". Not.

Sixth: "CCC[C@@](C1=CC=CC=C1)(C(=O)N)O". That's a tertiary butyl? Contains carbonyl amide attached to tertiary carbon with phenyl. Could match carbonyl 166, O-CH (maybe 52). But there is no ethoxy.

Seventh: "CC(=C[C@H]1[C@@H](C1(C)C)C(=O)OC)C#N". Not.

Eighth: "CC1=C2CCCCC2=C(N1C)C(=O)O". Not.

Ninth: "COC(=O)CC1=CC=CC(=C1)CCN". That's ethyl ester (COC(=O)...) plus phenyl-CH2-CH2-N. Contains carbonyl ester (170). But formula? Let's compute: COC(=O) is ethoxy carbonyl (C3H5O2). Then CC1=... phenyl plus ethyl chain to N. Might be C13? Not.

Tenth: "COC1=CC=CC2=C1CCN2CCO". Not.

Eleventh: "CC(C1=CC=CC=C1C(=O)CCN)O". This is a phenyl with carbonyl-CH2-CH2-N, plus tertiary alcohol? Contains O in side chain.

Twelfth: "C1C(OC(O1)C2=CC=CC=C2)CCN". Not.

Thirteenth: "CC1(CCN(C1)C2=CC=CC=C2O)O". Not.

Fourteenth: "CCC1=C(C=CC2=C1C(CCO2)N)O". Not.

Fifteenth: "COC1=CC=C2CCC/C(=N\\O)/C2C1". Not.

Sixteenth: "C[C@@H]1C=C1C2C(C2NC(=O)C(=O)C)C". Not.

Seventeenth: "C1CC1N2CCC(C2)(C3=COC=C3)O". Not.

Eighteenth: "CCOC(=O)C(C)C1=C(N=CC=C1)C". That's ethyl ester of something with pyridine.

Nineteenth: "C1=CC(=CC=C1CCC(=O)O)CCN". That's phenyl-CH2-CH2-COOH plus amine.

Twentieth: "CNC1(CC1)C2=C(C(=CC=C2)OC)O". Not.

We need C11H15NO2. Let's compute formula for candidate 6: "CCC[C@@](C1=CC=CC=C1)(C(=O)N)O". Count: phenyl C6H5, plus carbonyl C=O (C1 O1), plus N (N1), plus O (hydroxyl) O1, plus side chain: C4 (butyl) plus maybe extra carbon? Let's count: "CCC[C@@]" is butyl (C4H9). The chiral carbon attached to phenyl, carbonyl amide, OH, and butyl? Actually the chiral carbon is quaternary? Let's count atoms: string: C C C C [C@@](C1=CC=CC=C1)(C(=O)N)O. So central carbon attached to butyl chain (C4), phenyl (C6), carbonyl amide (C=O + N), and OH. So total carbons: butyl 4 + phenyl 6 + carbonyl carbon 1 = 11. Yes C11. Hydrogens: butyl C4H9, phenyl C6H5, central carbon has no H, carbonyl carbon none, OH adds H, amide N maybe H? The amide is C(=O)N (no H on N? Actually N has H? In SMILES "N" default has H? It would be NH. So N has one H. So total H: 9+5+1 (OH) +1 (NH) =16? Wait OH hydrogen counted as part of O? O has H. So 9+5+1+1 =16. But formula says H15. Maybe central carbon is attached to butyl chain which includes CH3-CH2-CH2-CH2? That's C4H9. Yes. So total H maybe 9+5+1 (OH) +1 (NH) =16. So formula C11H16NO2. Slight off.

Our experimental formula C11H15NO2 (odd H). Could be unsaturation (DBE). Let's compute DBE: C - H/2 + N/2 +1 = 11 - 15/2 + 1/2 +1 = 11 -7.5 +0.5 +1 =5. So DBE=5. For aromatic ring (4 DBE) plus carbonyl (1) =5. So consistent with phenyl + carbonyl amide, no extra ring.

Thus structure likely phenyl amide with ethoxy group? Wait ethoxy adds O and 2C, but we already have 11 carbons.

Phenyl (6) + carbonyl carbon (1) + ethoxy (2) =9, need 2 more carbons maybe in side chain attached to N (e.g., N-ethyl). That would be N-CH2-CH3 (2 carbons). So overall: phenyl-CO-O-CH2-CH3 (ethyl ester) but with N-ethyl? Actually amide: O=C(NCC)OCH2CH3? That's ethyl N-ethyl amide of benzoic acid: ethyl N-ethyl benzamide. Formula: C11H15NO2? Let's compute: benzamide C7H7NO (C6H5-CO-NH2) is C7H7NO? Actually C6H5-CO-NH2 = C7H7NO. Add ethyl group on carbonyl oxygen (making ethyl carbamate) gives C9H11NO2? Wait ethyl carbamate of benzoic acid: C6H5-CO-O-CH2CH3 (ethyl benzoate) is C9H10O2 (no N). Adding N-ethyl to amide: C6H5-CO-NH-CH2CH3 (ethyl phenylacetamide?) That's C9H11NO? Not.

Our formula includes two oxygens, one nitrogen. So could be an amide with an ethoxy substituent on carbonyl (i.e., a carbamate) where N is attached to phenyl? Example: phenyl carbamate: O=C(OC2H5)N-Ph. That's C9? Let's compute: phenyl (C6H5) + carbonyl carbon (1) + O (1) + ethoxy (C2H5O) = total C9? Actually carbon count: phenyl 6, carbonyl carbon 1, ethoxy carbon 2 =9. So C9. Not enough.

What about N-ethyl phenyl carbamate: O=C(OC2H5)N-CH2CH3-Ph? Wait N attached to ethyl and phenyl? That would be O=C(OC2H5)N(C2H5)Ph? That adds extra carbon (ethyl) to N, making C11. So structure: phenyl N-ethyl carbamate with ethoxy on carbonyl. SMILES: CCOC(=O)N(CC)c1ccccc1. Let's compute formula: CCOC(=O)N(CC)c1ccccc1. Carbons: ethoxy (2) + carbonyl carbon (1) + N-ethyl (2) + phenyl (6) =11. Hydrogens: ethoxy CH3CH2O: 5 H, carbonyl none, N-ethyl CH2CH3: 5 H, phenyl 5 H =15. Yes matches C11H15NO2. Good! So candidate SMILES: "CCOC(=O)N(CC)c1ccccc1". Let's validate.
